analysis.title: China AI: The Offshore Compute Door Closes; Inference Abroad, Not Domestic Cloud, Pays the Price
key_insights: On 16 November the US Commerce Department released an interim final rule extending chip controls to data centers worldwide. Any facility supplying more than 12mn aggregate TPP to a China-headquartered company needs a license, and the rule covers running models as well as training them.

JPM estimates the 12mn TPP threshold equals fewer than 800 H100-equivalents. The key change is that controls now reach inference served from abroad, which Chinese AI products use to reach global users.
JPM expects the news to weigh on China AI stocks broadly in the near term. It would buy the weakness in Alibaba, Tencent and Z.AI and expects MiniMax, whose exposure is direct, to underperform.

Chinese cloud providers that already hold capacity should see demand return from overseas, lifting utilization and pricing. The rule covers China-headquartered cloud providers operating abroad, but JPM estimates AliCloud's overseas AI revenue at below 10% of cloud revenue, so the direct revenue impact is small.

JPM's expectation of continued AliCloud revenue acceleration is in line with consensus. The rule changes the driver: with tighter foundry and packaging checks on China-designed chips and stronger competition for domestic accelerators, chip supply, not customer demand, now sets AliCloud's growth.

JPM says the market treats the rule as a pretraining constraint on all independent model developers. In its analysis, a company's exposure depends on how much of its training and inference runs on offshore compute.

Z.AI earns over 80% of revenue in China and is already on the Entity List. JPM believes its use of overseas compute for training and inference is very limited, so the rule adds little new restriction.

MiniMax earned about 60.8% of 1H26 revenue overseas, but not all of it is served on overseas compute. Where it is, the inference impact is direct because its generative products do not qualify for the recommender-system exclusion.

MiniMax can mitigate by serving overseas demand from domestic compute and by shifting to an asset-light, revenue-sharing model where overseas CSPs host and distribute its models. It does not disclose how much training runs overseas, which is the main unknown in sizing exposure.
Tencent is better placed because its advertising and content-recommendation workloads run mainly in China, and workloads abroad that only do recommendation are exempt.
Ratings are maintained at Overweight on Alibaba, Z.AI and Tencent and Neutral on MiniMax.
Rising domestic GPU rental and API prices would confirm JPM's thesis. MiniMax would become more attractive if BIS licenses its offshore compute providers.

market_movers.rationale: Overseas AI revenue is below 10% of AliCloud revenue, so direct impact is small. Returning overseas demand lifts utilization and pricing, though chip supply now caps growth.
Tencent (0700.HK): advertising and recommendation workloads run mainly in China, and recommendation-only workloads abroad are exempt.
Z.AI (2513.HK): over 80% of revenue is in China and it is already on the Entity List, so the rule adds little new restriction.
MiniMax (0100.HK): about 60.8% of 1H26 revenue is overseas and its generative products are not exempt, so inference impact is direct where served on offshore compute.

trade_ideas.description: Buy the weakness in Alibaba, Tencent and Z.AI after the US offshore compute rule
trade_ideas.rationale: The cost of the rule falls on inference served abroad, not on domestic cloud, and returning overseas demand lifts utilization and pricing for providers with capacity.
trade_ideas.risk: AliCloud capacity additions lag, a narrower recommender exemption for Tencent, or sustained increases in domestic compute rental costs for Z.AI.

trade_ideas.description: Expect MiniMax to underperform on direct exposure to the rule
trade_ideas.rationale: Its generative products do not qualify for the recommender-system exclusion and about 60.8% of 1H26 revenue is overseas.
trade_ideas.risk: BIS licenses its offshore compute providers.

risk_factors: AliCloud capacity additions lag through capex shortfalls or China-designed accelerators held at overseas foundries, so higher prices would lift margins but not revenue
Sustained increases in domestic compute rental costs would pressure Z.AI's gross margin
A narrower recommender exemption for Tencent, with the preamble's separate 90-day licence language for recommender services needing BIS clarification
MiniMax does not disclose how much of its training runs overseas, so exposure is hard to size
geopolitical: US Commerce Department interim final rule of 16 November extends chip export controls to data centers worldwide, requiring a license for facilities supplying more than 12mn aggregate TPP to China-headquartered companies
Z.AI is already on the US Entity List
Tighter foundry and packaging checks on China-designed chips

tension_points.bull_case: The cost falls on inference served abroad, not on domestic cloud. Demand returning from overseas lifts utilization and pricing for Chinese cloud providers that already hold capacity, and AliCloud's overseas AI revenue is below 10% of its cloud revenue.
tension_points.bear_case: Chip supply now caps AliCloud growth given tighter foundry and packaging checks and stronger competition for domestic accelerators. MiniMax has direct exposure because its generative products are not exempt and about 60.8% of 1H26 revenue is overseas.
tension_points.what_invalidates: AliCloud's capacity additions lag, through capex shortfalls or China-designed accelerators held at overseas foundries.

theme_stances.key_argument: The market treats the rule as a pretraining constraint on all developers, but exposure depends on how much training and inference runs on offshore compute.
theme_stances.evidence: falls on generative AI inference served abroad, not on domestic cloud
